summary:
Jonah son of Amittai appears once elsewhere in the Old Testament: 2 Kings 14:25 names him "the prophet from Gath-hepher" in Galilee, under Jeroboam II (mid-700s BC). Here God sends him east: "Get up! Go to the great city of Nineveh and preach against it, because its wickedness has come up before Me" (1:2). Nineveh was a major Assyrian city, later the empire's capital; Assyria would destroy Israel in 722 BC. Jonah sails the other way, "to flee to Tarshish, away from the presence of the LORD" (1:3). Unlike the other prophetic books, which mostly collect a prophet's messages, Jonah is a story about the prophet.

The LORD "hurled a great wind upon the sea" (1:4). The sailors each cry to their own god; the lot falls on Jonah, and at his own word they throw him overboard, though they first row hard for land. The sea calms; the sailors offer sacrifice and vows to the LORD (1:16). "Now the LORD had appointed a great fish to swallow Jonah" (1:17); from its belly Jonah prays a thanksgiving ending "Salvation is from the LORD!" (2:9), and the fish vomits him onto dry land.

Sent a second time, Jonah goes. His recorded sermon is five Hebrew words — "Forty more days and Nineveh will be overturned!" (3:4) — with no call to repentance and no offer of mercy. The city believes God and proclaims a fast; the king leaves his throne for sackcloth (coarse mourning cloth) and ashes: "Who knows? God may turn and relent" (3:9). God does — just what Jonah fled. His angry prayer quotes God's self-description at Sinai (Exodus 34:6): "I knew that You are a gracious and compassionate God, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion — One who relents from sending disaster" (4:2). As God "appointed" the fish, He now appoints a vine to shade Jonah, a worm to kill it, and a scorching east wind, then asks the closing question, unanswered: "So should I not care about the great city of Nineveh, which has more than 120,000 people who cannot tell their right hand from their left, and many cattle as well?" (4:11).

When it was written and how to read it are debated — history for some, a parable-like teaching story for others, and it is often read as satire: a pagan captain has to tell the prophet to get up and pray (1:6), the king's decree puts sackcloth on the animals (3:8), and Jonah grieves the death of a plant after resenting the rescue of a city. The text does not settle it. Jesus points to Jonah's three days and nights in the fish as the pattern for the Son of Man's "three days and three nights in the heart of the earth," and to Nineveh's repentance (Matthew 12:39–41; Luke 11:29–32).
